newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan state doctors and engineers threaten strike.
newsitem.headline: Jordan state doctors and engineers threaten strike.

text.p: Jordan's large public sector engineers and doctors unions said on Wednesday they plan to stage nationwide strikes this month if the government ignores long-standing pay demands.

Union officials in the Islamist-dominated Jordanian Engineers Association said they will stage strike action this month if demands of its 6,000 public sector members for nearly 20 percent rises in salaries are not met.
An emergency meeting of the union's annual general assembly on Friday called to discuss their pay demands agreed to stage a sit-in on Saturday in front of the Prime Ministry.

The union, with 26,000 members in total, agreed to escalate industrial action to a full scale strike if the government continued to ignore long simmering pay demands that go back to the 1980s, they said.
Unionists say starting salaries for graduates -- 270 dinars ($381) for general practitioners, 400 dinars for specialist doctors and 215 dinars for graduate engineers -- are too low.
"Prices are too high...and salaries of engineers whether state employees or private sector are not enough to cover the basic cost of living," said Hisham Khraisat, a union activist.
The doctors association, with a 11,000-strong membership, is also threatening strike action on October 26, calling for similar pay demands for its 2,800 public-sector colleagues, union sources said.
"The salary of a general practitioner is at the poverty level, if not below," said Basem Kasayani, heading the ministry of health's union committee.
Many Jordanians complain of a steep decline in living standards and express disappointment at dashed hopes of better economic conditions in the wake of Jordan's peace treaty with Israel in 1994.
Steep bread price hikes last August that sparked civil unrest are blamed by many Jordanians for having a spiral effect on a long list of basic consumer items.

Public sector employees who form nearly half an estimated 900,000 workforce complain that annual salary rises of well under 10 percent in the last few years have fallen far behind consumer price hikes.
Officially inflation is between three to four percent but independant estimates put it in double digits.
